query: For additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components, what single intervention could improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the current fabrication baseline, defines the processing and application conditions under which it should hold, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing an in situ preheating step during additive manufacturing of high-entropy alloy components will reduce thermal gradients, thereby lessening residual stresses and promoting a more uniform microstructure that improves dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects.
generation.material_initial_state: HEA components produced via conventional AM methods without preheating, which typically exhibit rapid cooling-induced thermal gradients, residual stresses, dimensional distortions, and microstructural defects such as porosity and microcracks.
generation.intervention: In situ preheating of the build chamber and/or substrate during layer-by-layer deposition.
generation.conditions: The preheating should be applied under standard AM processing conditions (e.g., selective laser melting or direct energy deposition) in an inert atmosphere, with optimized laser power and scan speed settings for both simple and complex HEA geometries.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduced temperature differentials during deposition lead to lower cooling rates, thereby diminishing residual stress buildup and refining the microstructure.
generation.mechanism: Preheating moderates the thermal gradient between successive layers, which slows down rapid and uneven solidification. This controlled cooling minimizes residual stress development and reduces the nucleation of defects such as pores and microcracks, resulting in components with improved geometry and mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a non-preheated baseline, components fabricated with in situ preheating will exhibit enhanced dimensional accuracy (with reduced warping and shrinkage), improved mechanical integrity (featuring higher strength and ductility), and a lower occurrence of fabrication-induced defects.
generation.baseline: Conventional AM-fabricated HEA components produced at ambient build temperatures, typically showing significant thermal gradients, higher residual stresses, dimensional inaccuracies, and increased defect density.
generation.boundary: The benefits of preheating depend on careful temperature optimization; insufficient preheating may fail to mitigate defects, while excessive preheating may risk issues such as grain coarsening or unwanted phase transformations. The efficacy may also vary with the specific high-entropy alloy composition and AM parameters.
generation.uncertainty: While improvements are expected, the precise magnitude of enhancement in dimensional precision and mechanical properties is uncertain and likely varies with alloy composition and processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of high-entropy alloy samples using an identical AM process and processing parameters, with one set produced using an optimized in situ preheating protocol and the other set fabricated at ambient temperature. Ensure that both sets have identical geometry, alloy composition, and environmental conditions.
measurements: Dimensional accuracy (quantitative assessment of warping, shrinkage, and geometric deviations via coordinate metrology or 3D scanning)
Microstructural analysis (scanning electron microscopy or X-ray tomography to assess defect density such as porosity and microcracks)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the preheated samples do not show statistically significant improvements in dimensional precision, mechanical integrity, and defect reduction compared to the non-preheated baseline, then the hypothesis that in situ preheating enhances dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Given the tight coupling between thermal histories, thermo-physical properties, and defect-inducing phenomena, varying process parameters affect the likelihood of specific printing defects. Thus, printability maps serve as valuable tools to identify defect-prone process parameter combinations, delineate at-risk regions, and guide the selection of optimal conditions to enhance AM design (see Fig. 1). These maps incorporate the maximum hatch spacing (Equation (13) in Table 7), which the melt pool geometry determines to ensure sufficient overlap between tracks in multi-scan prints. In this work, however, we focus solely on single-track scenarios, even though prior studies have shown that single-track printability maps can effectively identify optimal processing windows for fabricating defect-free 3D coupons and more complex testing specimens.

The study was subject to a few limitations, the foremost of which was the absence of pre-alloyed powder of the desired chemical composition. Thus, mechanical alloyed powder was used instead, which had a few drawbacks of its own. Only small powder quantities with comparatively coarse particle sizes could be established. Therefore, a small PBF-LB machinery able to cope with these conditions was employed, but it lacked the ability to preheat the fabrication chamber. Despite these difficulties, however, the CrFeNiTi MPEA was successfully processed by means of PBF-LB, and samples with large defect-free sections were produced. This serves as a good indicator that this type of alloy is suitable for the PBF-LB process, and with better processing circumstances, significantly larger, defect-free samples should be attainable.

drafts.hypothesis: In-situ substrate preheating during the additive manufacturing process of high-entropy alloys improves dimensional precision and mechanical integrity by reducing thermal gradients and residual stresses that lead to fabrication-induced defects.
drafts.material_initial_state: As-printed high-entropy alloy components typically show high residual stress, significant thermal gradients, and a non-uniform microstructure with defects such as micro-pores and cracks due to rapid cooling.
drafts.intervention: Introduce controlled in-situ preheating of the substrate (build plate) during printing.
drafts.conditions: Apply in a standard powder-bed fusion system with laser scanning, maintaining the build plate at an elevated temperature (e.g., within a range of 200°C to 400°C, optimized for the specific alloy) while keeping other printing parameters constant. The process should be conducted in a controlled atmosphere to minimize oxidation.
drafts.structural_mediator: Reduced thermal gradients and moderated cooling rates foster a more uniform microstructure with lower residual stress accumulation, thereby decreasing the formation of defects.
drafts.mechanism: The elevated substrate temperature lessens the abrupt thermal shock experienced by the deposited material, reducing the steep thermal gradients that typically induce residual stresses and microstructural inhomogeneity. This thermal moderation leads to fewer defects such as pores and cracks and improves inter-layer bonding, which in turn enhances overall dimensional precision and mechanical properties.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the conventional process at ambient build plate temperature, preheating is expected to yield components with improved dimensional accuracy and a meaningful increase (on the order of approximately 10–20%) in mechanical strength, accompanied by a lower density of fabrication-induced defects.
drafts.baseline: The current additive manufacturing process performed under ambient build plate conditions with standard laser scanning parameters.
drafts.boundary: This intervention is expected to be beneficial as long as the preheat temperature is carefully optimized; insufficient preheating may not mitigate defects, while excessive preheating could introduce other issues such as grain coarsening or oxidation. The beneficial effect may also depend on the specific high-entropy alloy composition and printing speed regime.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a series of high-entropy alloy samples using additive manufacturing under identical conditions except for the build plate temperature. Use a range of preheat temperatures (including ambient as a control). Characterize dimensional accuracy using 3D metrology, mechanical integrity via tensile and fatigue tests, and defect density using scanning electron microscopy.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if samples produced with in-situ substrate preheating do not show statistically significant improvements in dimensional precision, mechanical properties, or a reduction in defect density compared to the control samples fabricated at ambient temperature.

drafts.hypothesis: Adaptive laser power modulation during layer deposition will improve dimensional precision, enhance mechanical integrity, and reduce fabrication-induced defects in additively manufactured high-entropy alloy components.
drafts.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy components fabricated via standard additive manufacturing processes, exhibiting residual thermal gradients, dimensional instabilities, and microstructural defects such as porosity and microcracks.
drafts.intervention: Implement adaptive laser power modulation in place of a fixed-power laser approach during the build process.
drafts.conditions: The process should be conducted in an inert atmosphere under standard additive manufacturing conditions with feature sizes between 1–10 mm; similar laser scanning strategies and powder feedstock properties as used in the current baseline.
drafts.structural_mediator: The real-time adjustment of laser power reduces peak thermal gradients and associated residual stresses during solidification.
drafts.mechanism: By adaptively modulating the laser power during deposition, the energy input is optimized in response to local thermal histories. This minimizes extreme temperature gradients and thermal stresses, leading to a more uniform microstructure with fewer porosity and cracking events, and thus improved dimensional accuracy and mechanical properties.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the current fixed-parameter baseline, components produced with adaptive laser power modulation will show reduced dimensional deviations, a lower density of fabrication-induced defects, and enhanced mechanical strength (with improvements possibly measurable as statistically significant differences in tensile strength and reduced residual stress levels).
drafts.baseline: Standard additive manufacturing using a fixed laser power setting, which typically results in notable thermal gradients, dimensional deviations, and defect formation in high-entropy alloys.
drafts.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective under typical build conditions and common high-entropy alloy compositions; its performance under extreme geometries, ultra-high precision components, or non-standard alloy systems has not been established.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of identical high-entropy alloy components under identical processing conditions except that one set is produced with the standard fixed laser power and the other with the adaptive laser power modulation. Use in-situ monitoring to document thermal profiles and post-process analysis to measure dimensional tolerances, defect density, and mechanical properties.
measurements: Residual stress profiles (via X-ray diffraction or other suitable techniques)
Porosity and micro-crack density (via optical/electron microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If components produced with adaptive laser power modulation do not show statistically significant improvements in dimensional precision, lower defect densities, and enhanced mechanical properties relative to components fabricated with fixed laser parameters, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Preheating the build chamber during additive manufacturing of high-entropy alloy components will decrease thermal gradients that otherwise cause rapid and uneven solidification, resulting in improved dimensional accuracy, enhanced mechanical integrity, and fewer process‐induced defects.
drafts.material_initial_state: Components fabricated via standard selective laser melting or similar AM processes without build chamber preheating, typically exhibiting residual thermal stresses, dimensional distortions (e.g., warping), and microstructural defects such as pores and microcracks.
drafts.intervention: Introduce an in situ preheating step by elevating the build chamber and/or substrate temperature during the layer-by-layer deposition process.
drafts.conditions: The intervention should be applied during typical AM processing (e.g., SLM or DED) under an inert atmosphere with controlled laser power and scan speed, and for both simple and geometrically complex high-entropy alloy parts.
drafts.structural_mediator: A reduced temperature differential during layer deposition leads to lower cooling rates, which minimizes residual stress buildup and promotes a more homogeneous and refined microstructure.
drafts.mechanism: Preheating lessens the abrupt thermal gradients that drive rapid solidification and uneven microstructure formation. This mitigates residual stresses and thermal distortion while suppressing defect (e.g., porosity, microcracks) nucleation, leading to more precise geometry and improved mechanical properties.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the non-preheated baseline, components produced with in situ preheating will exhibit improved dimensional precision (reduced warping and shrinkage), higher mechanical integrity (enhanced strength and ductility due to a more uniform microstructure), and a lower frequency of fabrication-induced defects.
drafts.baseline: AM-fabricated high-entropy alloy components made without preheating typically show significant thermal gradients, higher residual stresses, dimensional inaccuracies, and a greater density of defects.
drafts.boundary: The effectiveness of preheating will depend on the specific alloy composition and AM processing parameters. Excessive preheating may potentially lead to unwanted grain coarsening or overheating; thus, an optimal temperature range must be established. Additionally, other parameters (e.g., laser power and scan speed) may influence the overall benefit.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of additively manufactured high-entropy alloy samples using identical processing parameters except that one set is produced with an optimized preheating protocol (build chamber preheated to a predetermined temperature) and the other set without preheating. Ensure the geometry and alloy composition are identical in both sets.
measurements: Dimensional accuracy assessment (e.g., using coordinate measuring machine or 3D scanning) to quantify warping and shrinkage.
Mechanical testing (tensile tests, microhardness measurements) to evaluate strength and ductility.
Microstructural characterization (via SEM, X-ray tomography) for defect density (porosity, microcracks) and grain uniformity.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples fabricated with preheating do not show statistically significant improvements in dimensional precision (decreased geometrical distortion), mechanical performance (strength and ductility), and a reduced defect density compared to the non-preheated samples, then the hypothesis that in situ preheating improves dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Integrating a real‐time, multi-objective laser parameter optimization system into the AM process of high-entropy alloys will improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity by minimizing fabrication-induced defects.
drafts.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured high-entropy alloy components produced using fixed laser parameters that frequently exhibit porosity, lack-of-fusion, and minor dimensional inaccuracies.
drafts.intervention: Implement an in-situ sensor-driven feedback loop coupled with a multi-objective optimization algorithm that dynamically adjusts laser power, scanning speed, and hatch spacing during processing.
drafts.conditions: Selective laser melting (or laser cladding) of equiatomic CoCrFeNi-based high-entropy alloys under a controlled atmosphere, where process parameters are continuously optimized in real time.
drafts.structural_mediator: Achieving a more uniform melt pool, improved overlap of melt tracks, and refined microstructure—all of which reduce thermal gradients and residual stresses that typically generate defects.
drafts.mechanism: The adaptive adjustment of laser parameters maintains an optimal energy density and consistent track fusion, leading to reduced porosity and defects, better dimensional fidelity, and enhanced interlayer bonding.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the conventional fixed-parameter process, the intervention is expected to yield parts with lower defect densities, improved dimensional accuracy, and superior mechanical properties (e.g., higher tensile strength and hardness).
drafts.baseline: Current additive manufacturing processes for HEAs using static, pre-set laser parameters that produce components with detectable fabrication-induced defects and moderate mechanical performance.
drafts.boundary: This improvement is anticipated for HEA systems with thermal properties similar to CoCrFeNi alloys when processed under controlled environmental conditions; effectiveness may be limited if sensor feedback or algorithm responsiveness is insufficient.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of HEA components via laser additive manufacturing under identical environmental conditions and using the same feedstock. One set is produced using conventional fixed laser parameters, and the other using the integrated in-situ multi-objective optimization system with dynamic parameter adjustment.
measurements: Dimensional precision metrics: surface roughness, geometrical tolerances, and part dimensions (via optical metrology or CT scanning)
Defect density: quantification of porosity and lack-of-fusion defects (using X-ray computed tomography)
Mechanical integrity: tensile strength, hardness, and fatigue performance tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the optimized samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in defect density, or if there is no measurable improvement in geometric accuracy and mechanical properties compared to the fixed-parameter baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.
